title: Mara, you are seen
hook: Mara comes as an ox, a farmer, a voice of doubt; each time he is recognized (SN 4)
tomorrow: What does being a woman matter

segments.voice: Yesterday: a king's frown at a daughter's birth, and your line, a daughter may be better. Did something unexpected land? Today a whole chapter of disguises, and one sentence that ends every one. Day six hundred forty-two.

The monks have set their alms bowls out in the open to dry. An ox wanders toward them, big and clumsy. One monk says to another, that ox is going to break the bowls. On another day, a farmer walks past with a plow on his shoulder and a goad in his hand, asking if anyone's seen his oxen. On another, there's just a voice, whispering that you're wasting your life. Same visitor, every time, in a different coat. The Samyutta gives him a whole chapter. Today: Mara.
screen: `AN OX NEAR THE DRYING BOWLS.` → `A FARMER WITH A PLOW.` → `THE SAME VISITOR, NEW COAT.`

segments.voice: Mara is the tempter in the Buddhist texts, the one who wants beings to stay caught. His name comes from a root meaning death, and he's sometimes called the Evil One. The fourth chapter of the Connected Sayings is all Mara. Some two dozen short scenes, and they follow a pattern. Mara shows up, often in disguise. In one he's a huge elephant king in the dark. In one, a serpent. In the scene with the bowls, an ox. In another, a farmer, who argues that the eye and the ear and all the senses belong to him. Sometimes he's not a shape at all, just a voice: you're not really awake, why bother, go back to ordinary pleasures. And every time, the Buddha recognizes him. That's the turn. He doesn't fight, doesn't flee, doesn't argue for an hour. He knows: this is Mara. Often he says so, in a short verse. And then comes the line that closes scene after scene, almost like a refrain. Mara, realizing the Blessed One knows me, sad and disappointed, disappears right there. Being seen is enough. Read the chapter as a psychology and it's strikingly practical. Temptation rarely announces itself. It arrives as something ordinary, a heavy animal, a reasonable farmer, a sensible voice of doubt. The power lies in the disguise. Once it's named, much of that power is gone. Buddhist schools differ on how literally to take Mara. Many traditional readers take him as a real being, a deity of the desire realm. Many modern teachers read him as a picture of our own craving and fear. The texts can hold both.
screen: `MARA: THE ONE WHO KEEPS BEINGS CAUGHT` · `AN ELEPHANT, A SERPENT, AN OX, A FARMER` · `EVERY TIME, HE IS RECOGNIZED` · `THE BLESSED ONE KNOWS ME, AND HE GOES` · then, large: `I SEE YOU, MARA.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of one temptation that keeps visiting you. The extra scroll. The sharp reply. The voice that says skip it, it doesn't matter. Picture what disguise it usually wears: tired, reasonable, deserved. Now, quietly, or aloud if you're alone, name it. Just a plain sentence: I see you. Not angry. Not afraid. The way you'd recognize an old acquaintance at the door. Then let the breath carry on, and notice what happens to the pull once it's been named. The bell holds the time.
Mara. The tempter of the Buddhist texts, whose name means death; in SN 4 he comes in disguise again and again, and each time he is recognized and disappears. Today's word.
Your line: I see you, Mara. When a familiar temptation shows up today in its usual disguise, name it once, plainly, and watch what it does. Day six hundred forty-two.

screen: `DAY 642 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DOES BEING A WOMAN MATTER.`

howItsDone: Buddhist art across Asia shows Mara and his armies at the night of the awakening, and many meditation teachers encourage students to name distractions and cravings as they arise, sometimes playfully as visits from Mara.

fork.setup: you're a monk drying your bowl. an ox wanders toward the bowls, and your teacher says it's Mara in disguise. what does the chapter show as the answer?
options: chase the ox away with a stick.
see it clearly for what it is.
pack up the bowls and leave.
fork.reveal: in scene after scene, recognition is enough: Mara knows he's been seen, and disappears right there.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit Mara: the tempter, from a root meaning death, to die or to kill.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mara is a Buddhist devil.
what it means: the tempter of the texts, who keeps beings caught; in SN 4 he loses his power the moment he is recognized.

what a scholar hears: the Mara Samyutta gathers some twenty-five episodes; the refrain where he realizes he has been seen and vanishes closes many of them, and later traditions speak of several Maras, including the defilements and death itself.
